title: This GTA V mod lets you destroy Flock cameras. Its creator explains why. - Mashable
content: Los Santos has a new way to get you in trouble, and you don’t even have to commit a crime. A new Grand Theft Auto V mod from artist Morry Kolman, who goes by WTTDOTM online, installs 235 virtual Flock license plate reader cameras around the game’s fictional city. Called Grand Theft Automated License Plate Reader, or GTALPR, it brings an extra layer of surveillance to your next drive. And because this is GTA, you can destroy the cameras and collect in-game cash from their wreckage. But the opportunity to blow them up is only part of the point. Kolman wants players to feel what happens when a familiar environment becomes a place where they’re constantly being watched. "I’m an artist, and much of my practice is based around giving people interesting and engaging ways to learn about the technological and political world around them," Kolman told Mashable. "GTALPR is very much in that vein." For Kolman, a game modeled on an American city, and familiar to millions of players, offered a way to make surveillance tangible. "Suddenly, you're always watched," he added. "With the simple addition of some cameras, the entire environment gains a new passive layer of hostility." In the real world, Flock’s automated license plate readers capture vehicle images and enable police to search for vehicles and receive alerts about those on watchlists. Flock pitches the technology as a way to help law enforcement locate wanted vehicles. Civil liberties groups, including the ACLU, argue that these networks enable mass surveillance of people going about their everyday lives. Kolman’s virtual version draws directly from the geography of the real network. "I chose 235 for the number of cameras to use in GTALPR because it is 1/10th the amount of Flock cameras currently in LA County, and Los Santos is about 1/10th its real counterparts size," he told Mashable. His project page identifies the community mapping project DeFlock as the source for the camera count. The placements aren’t random, either. Kolman built himself a tool to compare the real and fictional maps, then used it to place cameras in corresponding locations. "The closest comparison is probably the area around Santa Monica Pier vs. Del Perro Pier," he said. The result brings a real-world surveillance footprint into a place players may already know street by street. One of the mod’s most pointed feature kicks in when players haven’t committed a crime. Each time a player passes through a camera’s field of view, there’s a 1-in-20 chance it will trigger an unprovoked police chase to "represent this pattern of false reports, and show that living with this surveillance is not a matter of 'having nothing to hide'... it is simply a matter of 'when will it happen to you,'" Kolman described. His broader argument is that avoiding wrongdoing doesn’t eliminate the risks of being surveilled. He described the mechanic as a challenge to the familiar reassurance that people with "nothing to hide" have nothing to worry about. Players can also dismantle the virtual network. Destroy a camera and collect its remains, and the mod awards $600 in game currency. The reward price is based on the estimated value of the parts inside a real Flock camera, after the group Eyes Off Cedar Rapids took one apart to examine its hardware. There’s also built-in speedrun tracking for destroying the cameras, plus an option to render and save the images they capture — including pictures of players destroying them. It’s an absurd addition to a game already full of opportunities for mayhem, but a fitting one in a country where Flock cameras have made everyday drives part of a searchable surveillance network. As Kolman puts it, "I put Flock cameras in GTA V as a way to highlight and make tangible the pervasive intrusion of Flock and other ALPR cameras into daily American life via a game that is based on an American city and that millions of my fellow citizens are intimately familiar with." title: Fanatics, Players Associations, and Leagues Win Legal Case Similar to Panini v. Fanatics - Sports Illustrated
content: In major breaking hobby legal news, this morning, Fanatics, along with the MLB, NFL, and NBA and their players' associations, won a court ruling in Jones v. Fanatics, the closest copycat case to Panini v. Fanatics, with the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York denying claims of attempted monopolization under the Sherman Act and dismissing the consolidation case in its entirety, even before reaching discovery. It was dismissed by Chief U.S. District Judge Laura Taylor Swain, the same judge in the Panini v. Fanatics case. This was the second legal ruling Fanatics has won this year. Earlier in 2026, the same court and judge dismissed Scaturo v. Fanatics class-action lawsuit which was for direct purchases (through Topps.com). The ruling today dismissed a 13-count lawsuit against Fanatics, the player associations, and leagues that targeted indirect consumer purchases (say, through hobby shops and retail locations). This lawsuit was the consolidation of seven class-action lawsuits to narrow down the scope. The dismissal from Chief U.S. District Judge Laura Taylor Swain was a decision that failed to show consumer harm. From the decision: "Plaintiffs provide no market-wide analysis, data, or other evidence to support a finding of market-wide supracompetitive pricing. Their Reddit and YouTube sources, at best, convey the anecdotal experiences and opinions of different individuals." More from Judge Laura Taylor Swain: "Plaintiffs also fail to demonstrate an injury for purposes of Article III standing through their related claim that they purchased NBA cards of reduced quality as a result of Fanatics cutting off Panini’s supply of player jerseys for use in certain premium cards. This is because Plaintiffs, again, do not allege what cards they bought, let alone that any named Plaintiff purchased a premium card that suffered from their described jersey problem. Without allegations suggesting that any named Plaintiff suffered an injury related to these allegedly degraded cards, Plaintiffs cannot demonstrate an injury on these facts." It remains to be seen what this means in the case of Panini v. Fanatics. However, given that the same judge will hear the case, it likely weakens Panini's case against Fanatics. I'm not a lawyer, but it reads like the case against Fanatics was brought up hastily and clumsily, as the judge repeatedly had to say the plaintiffs did not actually suffer the consequences they alleged. Could another court case prove it? Who knows, but both cases brought against Fanatics didn't seem very strong. All while they weakened Panini's position in Panini v. Fanatics. title: CR-V Hybrid Owners Have 3 Questions Before the Next Model Arrives, But a 10% MPG Gain Only Catches the 43 MPG RAV4 - torquenews.com
content: Honda's next CR-V Hybrid could enter production as early as February 2027, according to Nikkei Asia, but owners on Reddit want head gasket answers before they get excited. If you are shopping now, the good news is that every 2026 CR-V Hybrid already carries 10 year, 150,000 mile head gasket coverage, and waiting may save you only about $100 a year in fuel. That is because Honda's promised 10 percent efficiency gain would only bring the CR-V Hybrid up to what a [2026 Toyota RAV4 Hybrid](INSERT: Tim's RAV4 XSE vs CR-V Hybrid story) already gets. Honda told Motor1 it has not announced the timing, so here are the 3 questions owners want answered, and what they mean for your decision. Honda says its next generation hybrids arrive starting in 2027, with a system built to use about 10 percent less fuel and cost about 30 percent less to produce. High gas prices are pushing more shoppers toward hybrids, which may be why Honda is moving faster, and why the current CR-V still makes a strong case for buying now. Question 1, Is the CR-V Hybrid Head Gasket Problem Fixed? This is the first question customers will need to ask of Honda. We’ve mentioned before that Honda has a technical service bulletin out for this issue, and the CR-V is among the models affected. The head-gasket problem can cause overheating, loss of coolant, and misfiring. One thing to bear in mind - if there’s a new hybrid design, it might use a different head-gasket design. Either way, it’s more likely than not that Honda will have addressed the issue and perhaps corrected it by now. That seems even more likely given that Honda extended warranties on older models to address the issue. If the company is willing to extend a warranty, it is likely looking to address the issue with a new engine so that it doesn’t crop up again. It’s more cost-effective for the company to make sure it’s not a problem with the new powertrain, and it will obviously be easier to sell 2027 CR-Vs if buyers aren’t worried about head-gasket failures down the line. Question 2, Will the Next CR-V Hybrid Beat the RAV4 Hybrid on MPG? Reddit users had concerns about fuel economy, and they want it to be better than what it is now. Here’s what one said: “10% of current 45 mpg would be 4.5mpg increase. So it's trying to get closer to 50mpg that the RAV4 already does. So a minor update. If I was in the market, I would want them to bring in the plug in variant in Europe. Would love to get 50 miles of EV capability which would be perfect for work commute.” As always, we edit these comments for content, clarity, and grammar. A few others chimed in with their own real-world fuel economy numbers. “You mean current 37 mpg,” one said. Another said “City estimate for our Sport Hybrid is 43 mpg.” Yet another said “I only hit that on the highway. Otherwise it's about 40-42mph in town.” The Honda CR-V Hybrid’s EPA-estimated fuel economy is 43 mpg city/36 mpg highway/40 mpg combined for front-wheel drive models and 40/34/37 for most all-wheel drive trims, with the number being 38/33/35. Question 3, Will the Next CR-V Hybrid Finally Get a Spare Tire? One Redditor, who seemed to be a car salesperson, suggested this: “The CRV would benefit greatly from a spare tire.” There was some pushback, and some agreement. One said “Statistically almost no one will ever use a spare. I’d much rather have more refined build than a spare. Two folks pushed back on that: “Specious logic. Most people will never ride in an ambulance, so should we just get rid of them? Any sidewall damage makes the fix-a-flat nonsense worthless. If you like to camp or live in a rural area then having a spare is important, and should at least be an option (if not standard). It at the very least should be designed into the available space/structure of the car.” And: “The probability that a driver will need a spare tire in their lifetime is nearly 100%. According to data compiled by the AAA and tire manufacturers, the average driver in the United States will experience up to five flat tires during their driving lifetime. With roughly 220 million flat tires occurring annually in the U.S. I think I’ve had five flat tires in my lifetime.” Most important, though, was this comment: “A lot of people including me didn't buy hybrid due to no spare...also even if someone can't change it they can call someone who can…big difference.” If the lack of a spare is costing sales, perhaps Honda will need to make sure the next CR-V hybrid has one. If you want or need a new car right now, and the CR-V is on your list, well, the choice is obvious: Buy now. If you can afford to wait, you can hang tight until the next CR-V is launched and check out the specs and see if the fuel-economy is improved. You can learn all about the new tech before signing on any dotted lines. As for the head-gasket issue, that might not be a problem with the next-gen CR-V Hybrid, but you can always check a vehicles’ VIN (vehicle identification number) and see if it’s been included in the TSB campaign. We’d do that with a 2026, since some 2026 model-year CR-Vs were affected. Finally, if having a spare tire matters to you, you can wait to see if Honda offers one. title: The Futuristic-Looking Hyundai Ioniq V Launches At Just $14,800 In China - Yahoo Autos
content: The Hyundai Ioniq V starts at $14,800 in China, under a limited-time promotion. The actual base price is closer to $16,500. That's a low price in China, beating some smaller cars. The Ioniq V uses CATL LFP battery and an 800-volt electrical architecture. Hyundai is on a roll. Around the world, the brand has a series of stylish EV models on sale at affordable prices. Perhaps the grass is greener on the other side, but I often find myself frustrated at the fact that there are so many cool Hyundai EVs that we won't ever get in the U.S. Case in point: the Hyundai Ioniq V. When the car was revealed this year at the Beijing Auto show, its Prius-meets-Lamborghini styling stood out, even in a room of hyper-advanced Chinese models. And maybe that was the point. Hyundai's new strategy to turn around its China business starts with the Ioniq V, the first of a series of cars developed in China, for that market. Now it's on sale. On Tuesday, Hyundai China officially launched the Ioniq V. At about $14,800, it's cheap—and not just by U.S. standards. Even in China, that's a very competitive price. Now, to be fair, that's a limited-time offer. Without that, the official price is around $16,500. It's a lot of car for the money, too. The Ioniq V is a midsize car, roughly the same size as the gas-powered Hyundai Sonata. But its pricing is on par with compact or even subcompact EV models from Chinese brands. For example, it costs about as much as the compact BYD Dolphin. It is powered by either a 188-horsepower or 225-horsepower motor turning the front wheels. The less powerful motor is fed by a CATL-sourced 53.5 kWh LFP battery, good for 335 miles (540 km) of estimated range. The larger motor is fed by a 66.8 kWh LFP battery, good for 404 miles (650 km). These numbers are both according to China's generous CLTC cycle, so expect these ranges to drop if the Ioniq V ever leaves China. It does use Hyundai's E-GMP 800-volt platform, but no charging times have been specified yet. The Ioniq V has a full suite of driver-assistance features developed with China's Momenta. There's an infotainment screen that takes up much of the Ioniq V's width, running on a Qualcomm Snapdragon 8295P system-on-a-chip. This is fancy stuff for such a cheap car here in the U.S., but it's pretty common in China. While many foreign brands have lagged behind Chinese rivals, Hyundai is clearly trying to beat China at its own game, offering a feature-packed car at a budget price. At the Beijing Auto Show in April, Hyundai CEO José Muñoz committed to staying in the Chinese market and said the company was "tripling down" on it. With such an aggressive pricing strategy for the Ioniq V—and a car that looks to match homegrown rivals on tech and value—it looks like this brand means business. The Hyundai Ioniq V Looks Great. title: USWNT roster: Ashley Sanchez earns the call for friendlies v Spain - The Guardian
content: Sanchez, NWSL’s top scorer, returns after years away Naomi Girma called up despite injury absence for Chelsea Naomi Girma and Sam Coffey are returning to the United States women’s national team, with their pair of WSL standouts named in Emma Hayes’ squad for October’s friendlies against defending World Cup champion Spain. NWSL top scorer Ashley Sanchez has also earned a recall on the back of her MVP-caliber performance with the North Carolina Courage. Sanchez has already set an league record for goals in a season by an American player, already up to 20 in 26 matches. With another goal, Sanchez will break Temwa Chawinga’s overall scoring record. An attacking midfielder, Sanchez’s most recent cap came in October 2024, in a friendly against Argentina early in Hayes’ tenure. Hayes largely leaned on established members of her core for the 26-player squad, adding four uncapped players on the back of strong seasons in the NWSL. “While we are very much looking forward to playing the World Cup champions, I keep coming back to the journey that we are all on together,” said Hayes. “This camp will be about reestablishing connections after a long break, looking at a few players who haven’t been with us this cycle, and putting on the best performances we can in front of packed stadiums.” Sanchez’s recall has been a hot topic in NWSL circles as the playmaker continues a career year. A member of the 2023 Women’s World Cup squad, Sanchez failed to get on the field that summer and has since been a peripheral figure as positional alternatives like Lavelle, Jaedyn Shaw, and Croix Bethune have been preferred by Hayes. Sanchez’ recall may help explain the absence of Shaw, whose brace over the weekend brought her to nine goals for Gotham this season. Shaw has been a regular part of the national team setup following the last World Cup, with 17 caps earned in the explorational 2024 and 16 more caps since the start of 2025. The question this window, and in subsequent ones, is how much of Sanchez’s stellar performance with North Carolina will carry over with the national team. The Courage’s team is built to cater to her strengths, allowing her to serve as chief facilitator as well as the team’s primary scoring threat. Hayes’ team already has plenty of players who are comfortable with those responsibilities, and while no team can ever have too many decisive game-breaking options in the final third, it’ll be up to the coaching staff and Sanchez to find the right way to maximize her considerable threat. Also among those selected is Mallory Swanson, who was involved in the team’s June camp but who didn’t see the field in two contentious friendlies against Brazil. Her last cap for the national team was her goal-scoring, gold medal-winning showing in the 2024 Olympic final. Swanson has appeared in just one of the struggling Chicago Stars’ five most recent games as she works back from injury and the birth of her daughter late last year, but earned Hayes’ faith while co-headlining the Olympic team with fellow “Triple Espresso” front-liners Trinity Rodman and Sophia Wilson – both also selected for the October friendlies. All eight defenders selected have made at least seven appearances for the USWNT, including young options like Kennedy Wesley, Gisele Thompson, and Lilly Reale. Girma’s return should help refine the team’s play in the defensive third and give a vital primary focal point in possession sequences, as Girma often leads the team in touches whenever available. However, she will be lacking in match fitness, having not appeared for Chelsea due to injury since early September. Emily Fox, Tierna Davidson, Tara Rudd, and Avery Patterson round out the options along the backline. Coffey will offer similar stability at the base of midfield, giving Hayes all of her most leaned-upon options for this window. Lindsey Heaps arrives with 178 caps to her name, having been in and out of availability since joining expansion Denver Summit this summer. Claire Hutton and Lily Yohannes have emerged as regular contributors since the Olympics, while Rose Lavelle remains in fine form for Gotham. Notably, the team listed Swanson among the midfielders and Sanchez among the forwards. Rodman, Swanson, and Wilson are again the attackers in focus, but Alyssa Thompson will look to fortify her case to be Hayes’ starting left winger. The Los Angeles native played matchwinner over the weekend against Arsenal and complements Wilson and Rodman well, moving upfield with decisiveness and showing equal willingness to bait defenders into opening space for her teammates as she is to set up her own shot. Emma Sears and Michelle Cooper offer strong alternatives on the right wing. Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Jordan Silkowitz could earn her first cap in goal on the back of a strong season. The Bay FC goalkeeper ranks second in the NWSL with 10.4 goals prevented, a metric which compares her conceded goals to post-shot expected goals faced, and leads all NWSL goalkeepers in minutes played without misplaying a cross. She’ll vie for minutes against two of Hayes’ most trusted options in goal, Phallon Tullis-Joyce of Manchester United and Claudia Dickey of the Seattle Reign. The sole newcomer among the midfield septet is Evelyn Shores, who primarily features for Angel City as a left back. The 21-year-old is a threat to create chances with both chipped crosses and her corner kicks, and gives Hayes a needed extra option down the left flank. Two forwards could earn their debuts this window, too. Pietra Tordin has been electric in her second season with the Portland Thorns, with seven goals and nine assists in 2,086 minutes. Her partnership with Wilson has come together quickly, with Tordin benefitting from the additional focus Wilson commands from opponents. Trinity Byars also arrives without a senior cap to date, with the 23-year-old having scored 10 goals in just over 1,000 minutes for San Diego. The United States will play their first game against Spain in Washington DC on 10 October, before playing a second friendly on 13 October in Philadelphia. title: The V-10-powered Motorcycle Available in a Neiman Marcus Catalog - The ClassicCars.com Journal
content: 500-horse Viper engine, 300-mph top speed, 0 safety considerations If you attended the North American International Auto Show in Detroit in January 2003, you’d catch some really cool unveils like the Rolls-Royce Phantom, Aston Martin AMV8 Vantage, Ford Mustang GT coupe concept, and V-16-powered Cadillac Sixteen concept. Then, something unusual called the Dodge Tomahawk would mentally transport you into the plot of “Blade Runner” without your consent. The brochure for this motorcycle concept mentions that the original reaction to this vehicle “typically comes in two words: ‘wow’ and ‘why.’” Trevor Creed, then senior vice president of design at Chrysler Group, weighed in, saying, “Tomahawk as an icon of the extreme thinking for a brand that is known not only for the legendary Viper and Ram, but also for all new, innovative vehicles such as the Magnum SRT-8 and Durango concepts.” That same brochure touted the Tomahawk as “Breaking Boundaries at Full Throttle.” Now, I don’t remember 2003 as much as I should due to my age, but was boundaries another word for “bones” or “lifeforce?” This four-wheel, single-passenger motorcycle featured a 505ci V-10 sourced from a Viper, which was advertised at 500-plus horsepower and a top speed of “nearly 400 miles per hour — for anyone who wants to test it.” The engine was paired with a custom-made two-speed manual sequential racing transmission, four-wheel independent suspension, and absolutely zero regard for human life. I must admit, the rolling dystopian look Dodge brought forward with this motorcycle somewhat intrigued me as a kid (and still does!), though there’s a pesky realization of “maybe going down the road with only a V-10 engine in-between your legs is dangerous” that brings me back to Earth. It looks like something either Rick Deckard (played by Harrison Ford) would drive in “Blade Runner,” or maybe something that would complement an evil Robocop nicely. In either case, whoever is driving would have to be the only one since, regretfully, Dodge only wanted one driver with a suicidal need for speed instead of a driver and passenger. Offered at $555,000 in the Neiman Marcus catalog, it is believed that up to nine were built for the general public, though it was sold as automotive sculpture, as opposed to a street-legal vehicle (wink-wink). “The replica is operational,” Dave Elshoff, senior manager for sales, marketing and motor-sports communications for the Chrysler group, told Forbes magazine, but “it is not fully road-tested and validated by our engineers.” Growing up, Corey Decker spent time with his dad in the garage building muscle cars as a hobby. He also acquired intimate familiarity with classics new and old as the lead Car Description Editor at AutoHunter.com before segueing into The ClassicCars.com Journal. In a previous life, he worked as a sportswriter and even scored the opportunity to cover the 2016 Olympics. title: Is Czech Republic v England on TV? Channel, kick-off time and how to watch Nations League clash - Yahoo Sports
content: England will look to bounce back from the disappointment of defeat to Spain over the weekend as they continue their Nations League campaign by heading to Prague to take on Czech Republic. There was plenty of good from the Three Lions in a rollercoaster clash with the world champions at a sold-out Wembley on Saturday evening but the defending was borderline negligent at points as they fell to a 3-2 loss. In his pre-match press conference ahead of the clash at the Fortuna Arena, Thomas Tuchel was adamant that "it's a bit early for a 'must win'" game but another loss will not only put a huge dent in England's Nations League hopes but raise further questions over the direction of the team under Tuchel himself. The frustration of the World Cup semi-final defeat to Argentina, and the bad taste created by Tuchel's substitutions in that loss, still loom large, so a palate-cleansing victory over a side led by new coach Santi Denia would be most welcome for fans. Here's everything you need to know about the clash. Czech Republic v England is due to kick off at 7.45pm BST on Tuesday 29 September at the Fortuna Arena in Prague. Viewers in the United Kingdom can watch the match live on ITV1, with coverage from 7pm BST. A live stream will be available via ITVX. Man City star Nico O'Reilly, who was guilty of a lax pass for Spain's second goal at the weekend, and fellow defender Ezri Konsa are both doubts for the fixture after missing training on the eve of the fixture. "They need to be assessed and take a decision Tuesday morning," said Tuchel of the duo's availability. "Ideally I would love to put the same team out there. I need to speak with the doctors, physios and the players themselves, see what is responsible and what's not, then let's see." Nico O'Reilly is a doubt for the game against the Czech Republic (Getty) The remaining 22 members of the squad were in group training as normal on Monday after Cole Palmer, Declan Rice, Marcus Rashford, Kobbie Mainoo and Tino Livramento all withdrew from the squad last month due to a mixture of injury and load management. Tuchel's comments potentially suggest minimal changes to the starting XI from the Spain clash, with the boss having confirmed after that game that James Trafford will continue in goal for the Czech Republic encounter, before Jordan Pickford takes the gloves for the remaining two matches in this international window. One decision could come at right-back as the German mulls whether to continue with Jarell Quansah or whether this is the right time to reintegrate Real Madrid's Trent Alexander-Arnold into the side. At left-back, Lewis Hall will likely come in if O'Reilly is unable to play, while Jarrad Branthwaite is an option instead of Konsa if required. title: Strange New Worlds Makes One of Star Trek V’s Weirdest Moments Make (Some) Sense - reactormag.com
content:
Strange New Worlds Makes One of Star Trek V’s Weirdest Moments Make (Some) Sense Science fiction. Fantasy. The universe. And related subjects. "Turned All To Silver Screens" by Madeline Ashby "Audit of the Collapse and Convalescence of Minds" by Renan Bernardo Published on September 29, 2026 Note: This article contains spoilers for Star Trek: Strange New Worlds Now that a respectable time has passed since the Star Trek: Strange New Worlds finale, it feels like it’s finally time to start talking about the numerous notable moments spread throughout “Tomorrow’s Enterprise.” Few of those moments are more fascinating to me than the relationship tease that helps make Star Trek V: The Final Frontier make slightly more sense. Let’s start with the Strange New Worlds of it all. That episode that sees Uhura travel one year into the future also suggests that, at some point in the future, Uhura and Scotty are in some kind of relationship. How serious it is seems to be up for some interpretation, but it’s clear that it was at least pretty passionate for however long it may have lasted. Because these events happen in the early days of Kirk’s command of the Enterprise (or some version of it) and because Scotty/Uhura isn’t really a thing in the TOS stories, we can reasonably assume that their relationship doesn’t really last all that long. Except that’s not entirely true. In Star Trek V: The Final Frontier, there is a memorable scene that sees Uhura and Scotty share a tender, seemingly romantic moment when they have a little time alone together. The intimacy between the two is not only obvious but conveyed in such a way that suggests this is hardly the first time that the two have snuck away to caress and flirt with each other. If anything, they act like they’ve been doing this for years despite the fact that the show and previous movies never even hinted they were a thing. Yet, this seemingly on again, off again thing is never really mentioned again. Now, there are a lot of weird things in Star Trek V, many of which are the result of William Shatner going more than a little mad with creative power and directing a story that, in its own ways, doesn’t shy away from the suggestion that Kirk may be something of a god himself. But the thing that makes Scotty/Uhura so fascinating are the unanswered questions surrounding it. Was this a case of Shatner (or the actors) having a little fun with the scene? Was there something between the two that people just didn’t pick up on? It’s a minor point that doesn’t really compare to the other oddities in the fifth Star Trek movie, but I’ll be damned if it hasn’t lingered on throughout the years. However, Strange New Worlds seemingly suggests that Scotty and Uhura have had brief flings in the past that have either continued over the years or linger in the hearts and minds of the two strongly enough to occasionally spark those old feelings. In fact, Strange New Worlds producer Henry Alonso Myers recently confirmed that the team wanted to make the Scotty/Uhura relationship more than a one-off oddity. “So there has always been a flirtation. It kind of came out more in the movies between the two of them: an implication that they had history, that they had something going on,” Myers tells TVLine. “What we were trying to do was just reach out and imagine a deeper version of the thing that didn’t get to make it on screen. On the original series, that was not a big concern of theirs. Scotty played probably more comically in that regard… We wanted to bring it to their current [versions]. She’s a real character with real stakes, real emotion, and we thought it would be nice to imply that the things that we had seen already had a purpose in the past.” That’s… actually a pretty satisfying explanation. The idea that Scotty and Uhura have always had a little something going on in the background but that it was simply not something that defined either of them in the grand scheme of everything going on feels true enough to both characters and is a surprisingly mature way to address something that was perhaps never meant to make sense. Now quick, someone ask Shatner if he has any memory of this moment or the reasoning behind it.

title: Ancelotti hails comeback v Australia: “We struggled, but showed class” - Yahoo Sports
content: Head coach Carlo Ancelotti praised the national team's ability to respond in Tuesday's (29) 4-2 win over Australia. In the match at Suncorp Stadium in Brisbane, Brazil opened the scoring through Vanderson, but saw the hosts take the lead. Goals from Raphinha in the first half and Bruno Guimarães and Vinicius Jr. after the break secured the victory. In a press conference, the coach explained that the Seleção faced difficulties during the match and said he was pleased with the team's second-half display, especially Bruno Guimarães' goal, which came from a beautiful passing move. "It was a good game. We had difficulties, but we also showed good quality in our play. They looked for good quality in their play as well. It's true that we had difficulties in the match. We started well, then dropped our rhythm a little. But in the second half, I think the team responded well — a fantastic goal, the third one, with a fantastic combination. We're happy," he said. title: 2028 Ram Ramcharger Is a Burly, Full-Size, V-8-Powered SUV Worth Waiting For - Car and Driver
content: The Ramcharger will see Ram expand into a new segment, with the SUV sharing bones with the Jeep Grand Wagoneer but focusing on V-8s. For the first time ever, the Ram brand will branch out from trucks and commercial vans with a new SUV. Set to use the Ramcharger name, which previously adorned a truck-based SUV in the ’70s and ’80s, the Ram SUV will be related to the full-size Jeep Grand Wagoneer. Instead of the Jeep’s luxurious chrome trim and smooth six-cylinder engines, the Ramcharger will take on a more aggressive appearance and will prioritize rumbling V-8 power. The SUV will also give existing Ram truck customers a more practical, comfortable option geared more towards family life, without sacrificing the ability to tow hefty loads. The Ram brand is among parent company Stellantis’ most profitable ventures. The Ram pickup truck is the bestselling vehicle Stellantis sells in the United States, so capitalizing on that success with a related SUV seems like a no-brainer. It will also give Stellantis a lower-priced alternative in the full-size space, filling the hole that was created after Jeep consolidated the Wagoneer and Grand Wagoneer into a single model with a larger focus on luxury. See all results for new 2028 Ram Ramcharger for sale near 23917 The Ramcharger will share its body-on-frame platform with the Ram 1500 pickup truck and the Jeep Grand Wagoneer. While the Ram truck uses a solid rear axle, the Grand Wagoneer features an independent rear suspension, and we think the Ramcharger will borrow the setup from the Jeep. Expect coil springs at all four corners on the entry-level versions, with optional air suspension that becomes standard on the higher trims. An off-road-focused variant, possibly using the Rebel name, with more rugged styling and a more capable suspension, possibly including a low-range transfer case, seems a likely challenger to the Chevy Tahoe Z71 and Ford Expedition Tremor. Despite sharing a chassis with the Grand Wagoneer, the Ramcharger will attempt to carve out its own niche by focusing on different powertrains. While the Grand Wagoneer is currently motivated by the Hurricane twin-turbocharged 3.0-liter inline-six, producing 420 horsepower, the Ramcharger’s lineup will instead center around V-8s, which Tim Kuniskis, who runs Stellantis’ American brands, confirmed in an interview with The Drive. We expect the Ramcharger to offer the 395-hp Hemi 5.7-liter V-8 as a base engine, and possibly the 470-hp Hemi 6.4-liter V-8 as an optional upgrade. At Stellantis Investor Day, the company also confirmed that the Ramcharger will eventually offer an SRT-badged performance variant. We expect this to be a twin to the bonkers Ram 1500 SRT TRX, and it will likely use the same supercharged 6.2-liter V-8, which cranks out 777 horsepower. Still, the Ramcharger may utilize a powertrain with fewer than eight cylinders. Jeep is supposed to soon finally launch a much-delayed range-extended plug-in hybrid version of the Grand Wagoneer, which uses the Pentastar 3.6-liter V-6 as a generator to charge a 92-kWh battery hooked up to dual electric motors that make 647 hp. When the Ramcharger was first announced back in late 2025, it was said to feature both internal-combustion and range-extender setups. While it’s possible that Ram’s focus has now shifted exclusively to V-8s, we still bet the PHEV powertrain will find its way into the Ramcharger eventually—that is, if Stellantis can finally get it off the ground first in the Grand Wagoneer and Ram 1500 REV. See all results for new 2028 Ram Ramcharger for sale near 23917 The Ramcharger will challenge the other American full-size SUVs, the Chevrolet Tahoe and Suburban and Ford Expedition, with the pricier trims facing off against the GMC Yukon. Other rivals include the Nissan Armada and Toyota Sequoia. Given that the Grand Wagoneer currently starts at almost $68,000, the Ramcharger could have too much overlap with its Jeep cousin if it isn’t distinguished enough by price, style, and powertrains. Given that Ram is mainly known for trucks and commercial vehicles, getting customers into dealerships to look at a more family-friendly SUV may also require extra effort from the marketing department, especially given how well established the full-size SUVs from GM and Ford already are. Lastly, rising gas prices could hamper the market for a large, V-8-powered SUV if they continue on the current trajectory instigated by the war between the United States and Iran. The Ramcharger is expected to go on sale in 2028, with pricing likely starting somewhere in the $60,000 range. The Ramcharger will be built alongside the Grand Wagoneer at the Warren Truck Assembly in Michigan. title: Major dance festival Terminal V to be held on banks of River Clyde - BBC
content: Electronic music festival Terminal V will be held on the banks of the River Clyde next year, as the event comes to Glasgow for the first time. Organisers EE Live announced earlier this year it was moving from Edinburgh to Glasgow for the festival's 10th anniversary in 2027, but did not reveal details of where in the city it would be held. Now Clydeside Live - a new dedicated open-air event space on the north bank of the river - has been confirmed as the location. The festival will run from Friday 4 to Sunday 6 June and marks the dance event's first fully outdoor Scottish festival. The new venue is intended to be able to host a varied programme of seasonal attractions and entertainment, including gigs, fan zones and sports events. Organisers Derek Martin and Simon McGrath said the location would let them build the popular festival "from the ground up". "The scale, the riverside setting and the industrial landscape around it feel completely aligned with Terminal V and give us the freedom to create something we simply couldn't have done before," they said. "We've seen venues like Silverworks Island [in London] demonstrate just how exciting these large-scale outdoor inner city spaces can be for electronic music, and we believe Clydeside Live has the potential to become one of the most exciting new outdoor event destinations in the UK. "For our 10th anniversary, we have the opportunity to build the festival from the ground up, rethink our stages and production for the setting and create an experience that feels distinctly Glasgow while still being unmistakably Terminal V." After launching as a one-day event at Edinburgh's Royal Highland Centre  in 2017, Terminal V has expanded to include events in London, Croatia and Australia. Organisers say more than 30% of ticket sales come from outside Scotland and that previous editions have contributed more than £5m to the local economy. Cinematographer Melissa Cofie says their purpose has evolved with the growth of platforms like TikTok. Parastoo Ahmadi was convicted of "offending public decency" after singing while wearing a sleeveless dress during a livestreamed concert. The heavy metal band will be joined by the US rock musician during their London show. Swift took home the big award for video of the year on a night when the original Queen of Pop performed. title: Symposium on Jurisdiction, Responsibility, and Temporality: Nicaragua v. Germany Before the ICJ - Temporality and Third-State Responsibility in Prolonged Occupations - Opinio Juris
content: In association with the International Commission of Jurists [Ihsan Adel is the Founder and Chair of Law for Palestine and an international lawyer currently pursuing a PhD in Germany.] The preliminary objections proceedings in Nicaragua v Germany raise a temporal question extending beyond that case: when an occupation lasts for decades and its legal character evolves over time, how should a court identify the “situations or facts” giving rise to a dispute concerning the obligations of third States? Germany’s Optional Clause declaration of 30 April 2008 accepts the jurisdiction of the International Court of Justice only over disputes arising after that date “with regard to situations or facts subsequent to this date”. Germany argues that significant aspects of Nicaragua’s case concern longstanding German policies and conduct towards Israel which predate the critical date and continued thereafter. On this view, the post-2008 conduct is merely the continuation of an older situation whose “source or real cause” predates Germany’s acceptance of jurisdiction. Nicaragua responds that its claims concern post-2008 situations and facts, including discrete German decisions taken after the critical date. This disagreement raises a question concerning the application of temporal limitations to prolonged occupations. Neither the historical commencement of an occupation nor that of a third State’s relationship with the occupying Power can necessarily determine the temporal location of every subsequent dispute. Prolonged occupations are factually continuous but need not be juridically static. This matters in two respects. First, an unlawful situation originating before the critical date may itself continue beyond it. Secondly, and more importantly, subsequent developments may alter the legal character of that continuing situation and, consequently, the obligations governing third States’ dealings with it. From the Source of Rights to the Source of the Dispute The starting point is Right of Passage over Indian Territory (Portugal v India), which concerned a temporal limitation closely resembling that in Germany’s declaration. India’s Optional Clause declaration excluded disputes arising before 5 February 1930 or “with regard to situations or facts” prior to that date (para. 199). Portugal’s claimed right of passage, and the historical practice from which it derived, long predated the critical date; India’s obstruction of passage occurred in 1954. The Court distinguished between situations or facts which “constitute the source of the rights claimed” and those “which are the source of the dispute”. Only the latter were relevant to the temporal reservation. A dispute may therefore presuppose an older legal relationship or historical situation without arising “with regard to” it. The Court emphasised that the dispute could not arise until all its constituent elements existed, including India’s obstruction of Portugal’s passage. The converse proposition emerges from Phosphates in Morocco and Certain Property (Liechtenstein v Germany). Subsequent events cannot establish temporal jurisdiction where they merely confirm, develop or give effect to a pre-critical-date situation constituting the real cause of the dispute. In Certain Property, post-critical-date German judicial decisions could not be separated from the earlier confiscations and legal regime governing the property concerned. The inquiry is therefore not an archaeological search for the earliest historical antecedent of a claim. Nor may jurisdiction be created simply by selecting the latest manifestation of an already constituted dispute. The question is whether post-critical-date facts merely continue or give effect to a fully constituted pre-critical-date situation, or are themselves legally operative in constituting or transforming the situation giving rise to the obligations and alleged breaches now in dispute. A first difficulty with Germany’s argument concerns wrongful acts of a continuing character. International law distinguishes between a completed act whose effects persist and a breach which itself continues. Article 14(2) ARSIWA provides that a breach having a continuing character extends throughout the period during which the act continues and remains inconsistent with the relevant obligation. The European Court of Human Rights’ judgment in Loizidou v Turkey illustrates the distinction. Although the territorial situation preventing the applicant’s enjoyment of her property originated before Turkey’s acceptance of the Court’s jurisdiction, the continuing denial of access to and control over that property persisted beyond the critical date. Its historical origin did not exhaust its temporal existence. The point is relevant to Nicaragua v Germany. In its 2024 Advisory Opinion, the ICJ characterised Israel’s unlawful continued presence in the Occupied Palestinian Territory as a “wrongful act of a continuing character” (para. 267). If the underlying unlawful situation continued beyond Germany’s critical date, the third-State obligations applicable in relation to that situation likewise remained relevant to Germany’s post-2008 conduct. Nicaragua’s case is, moreover, not confined to the continuing effects of pre-2008 German decisions. It relies upon successive post-critical-date authorisations for exports of weapons and military equipment; increased military export authorisations; military cooperation and procurement from Israeli arms manufacturers; and Germany’s failure to prevent German companies from participating in settlement-related infrastructure, exploitation of Palestinian natural resources and the supply of equipment facilitating discriminatory practices. Whether these allegations establish breaches is a question for the merits. For temporal purposes, the narrower point is that Nicaragua challenges Germany’s own conduct during the post-critical-date continuation of allegedly unlawful situations, not simply a German policy completed before 2008. Continuity, however, is only part of the answer. The more fundamental difficulty is that a prolonged occupation may not simply persist: subsequent developments may alter its juridical character, and the post-2008 facts should not simply be dealt as later manifestations of an already complete pre-2008 situation. The Court’s 2024 Advisory Opinion provides the conceptual basis. It held that prolongation does not, in itself, change an occupation’s status under international humanitarian law. At the same time, an occupying Power’s exercise of effective control must “at all times” remain consistent with the prohibition on territorial acquisition by force and the right to self-determination (para. 109). The legality of continued presence must therefore be assessed over time. An occupation may consequently remain an occupation while settlement expansion, territorial integration and fragmentation, appropriation of natural resources, extension of domestic law, demographic transformation and assertions of permanence alter the legal character of the occupying Power’s continued presence. In 2024, the Court assessed Israel’s policies and practices cumulatively and concluded that they entrenched permanent control, amounted to annexation of large parts of the Occupied Palestinian Territory and frustrated Palestinian self-determination. Those findings, in turn, informed its conclusion that Israel’s continued presence was unlawful. Namibia provides an instructive precedent for the consequences of such juridical change. South Africa’s physical presence did not commence when that presence became unlawful. What changed was its legal character following the termination of the Mandate and subsequent United Nations action. Once its continued presence was unlawful, consequences followed not only for South Africa but for other States, which were required to recognise its illegality and refrain from dealings implying recognition or lending support or assistance to it. Physical continuity therefore did not entail juridical continuity. The legal character of a prolonged occupation must be assessed throughout its duration, and changes in that character may alter the application of third-State obligations as the situation evolves. Not every development during an occupation creates a new legally operative situation. Mere passage of time does not. The critical question is whether post-critical-date facts are legally constitutive: whether they independently engage an obligation, contribute materially to satisfying the factual predicates of a primary rule, cross a legal threshold through cumulative conduct, or materially alter the juridical character of a continuing situation. Article 15 ARSIWA provides a useful analogy. Where a breach consists of a series of actions or omissions defined in aggregate as wrongful, a composite breach occurs only once sufficient conduct has accumulated to constitute the wrongful act. This does not mean that annexation or unlawful occupation must themselves be classified as composite acts under Article 15. Rather, the provision illustrates a broader temporal point: later conduct may be constitutive of an aggregate legal situation rather than merely another manifestation of a situation already completed. Settlement construction, for example, may independently violate international humanitarian law while simultaneously contributing, together with land appropriation, infrastructure, territorial integration and extension of domestic law, to annexation or permanent control. Similar cumulative reasoning may apply to systematic discrimination and the frustration of self-determination. Different obligations may accordingly possess different temporal predicates; there need not be a single date on which a prolonged occupation acquires the character of a “new situation”. This distinction matters in Nicaragua v Germany. Israel’s occupation, settlement policy and restrictions on Palestinian self-determination plainly predate 30 April 2008. The 2004 Wall Advisory Opinion had already found the settlements contrary to international law and held that the wall and associated regime severely impeded Palestinian self-determination. Yet the 2004 Opinion itself illustrates why the legal situation cannot simply be frozen at that point. The Court described the wall and associated regime as creating a fait accompli that “could well become permanent” and, if it did, would be tantamount to de facto annexation (para. 121). Twenty years later, the Court concluded that Israel’s policies and practices had entrenched permanent control and amounted to annexation of large parts of the territory. The blockade of the Gaza Strip and breakdown of a fragile ceasefire in 2008, which eventually led to Operation Cast Lead, the first in a series of major assaults on the Gaza Strip, marked a radical change in the situation on the ground. In the West Bank including East Jerusalem, settlement expansion, land appropriation, territorial fragmentation and the increasing integration of settlements and their infrastructure into Israel further entrenched Israeli control; the kinds of policies and practices upon which the Court later relied in finding annexation and permanent control. Important legal and institutional developments accompanied these changes. Security Council Resolution 2334 (2016) reaffirmed that the settlements have no legal validity and called upon all States to distinguish, “in their relevant dealings”, between Israel and the territories occupied since 1967, directly addressing third-State conduct. In 2017, the then UN Special Rapporteur on Palestine, Michael Lynk, issued a report warning that Israel’s continued settlement expansion and de facto annexation had transformed the longest-running modern military occupation into an illegal regime. In 2018, Israel’s Nation-State Basic Law provided that national self-determination in Israel is unique to the Jewish people and recognised the development of Jewish settlement as a national value. Whatever weight each development carries individually, together they form part of a post-critical-date factual and legal record that cannot be treated as temporally irrelevant merely because some constituent practices had earlier antecedents. The 2024 Advisory Opinion should therefore be understood, for present purposes, as the culmination rather than the commencement of this legal trajectory: an authoritative judicial assessment of policies and practices accumulated over time and of the legal character of the situation they had produced. Third-State Obligations and an Unchanged German Policy This brings the analysis back to Germany’s contention that its policies towards Israel did not fundamentally change after 2008. Even assuming that proposition, the legal conclusion does not follow. Germany’s conduct cannot be assessed in isolation from the situation towards which it was directed and the obligations applicable to Germany in those circumstances. An unchanged third-State policy can acquire different legal significance when the juridical character of the underlying situation changes. Indeed, the alleged breach may lie precisely in maintaining an unchanged policy towards a situation whose legal character has materially altered. Nor does this require retrospectively treating every German act since 2008 as assistance in maintaining an unlawful occupation. The analysis must remain date- and obligation-specific: what obligation bound Germany at the relevant time; what factual and legal situation engaged that obligation; and what German conduct allegedly breached it? Germany’s own position that export licences undergo individual governmental assessment further underscores that subsequent authorisations are discrete decisions taken in the circumstances prevailing at the time. The relevant question is therefore whether those assessments adequately reflected changes in the legal character of the situation and the obligations applicable to Germany at the time of each decision. That inquiry must ultimately be conducted claim by claim. This approach is reflected in Judge Charlesworth’s question at the close of the September 2026 hearings, asking Nicaragua to identify, for each of submissions 4 to 9, the situations or facts constituting the “source or real cause” of its dispute with Germany in light of the temporal limitation in Germany’s declaration. Nicaragua v Germany therefore raises a broader question about how international law treats time in prolonged unlawful situations. The critical date cannot freeze either the legal character of an evolving situation or the obligations of third States in relation to it. What matters is not simply when the underlying situation began, but whether it continued, how it developed, and what legal significance those developments had: contribute to cumulative legal thresholds or alter the juridical character of a continuing situation and thereby the application of third-State obligations. The broader implication is that third-State obligations cannot be discharged through a once-and-for-all assessment of a situation or of relations with a State involved in it. Where changes in that situation engage or alter the application of international obligations, states maintaining military, economic or other relevant relations must assess those developments on an ongoing basis and, where required, adjust their conduct accordingly. This is particularly important in prolonged occupations -whether unlawful from their inception or becoming unlawful through subsequent developments- as well as in situations involving continuing violations of international humanitarian law or systematic racial discrimination. ©  Opinio Juris | Design by Open & Honest | In association with the International Commission of Jurists

title: Symposium on Jurisdiction, Responsibility, and Temporality: Nicaragua v. Germany Before the ICJ - Nicaragua’s Monetary Gold Problem (and its Solution) - Opinio Juris
content: In association with the International Commission of Jurists [Adil Ahmad Haque is a Distinguished Professor of Law and Judge Jon O. Newman Scholar at Rutgers Law School.] In its Preliminary Objections, Germany argues that Nicaragua’s claims are inadmissible because their resolution would require the Court to find Israel responsible for illegal conduct in its absence and without its consent. In its prior cases, namely Monetary Gold and East Timor, the Court declined to exercise its jurisdiction when it would have to rule on the legal rights or responsibility of an absent State as a prerequisite to ruling on the legal rights or responsibility of the parties to the case. In such cases, the legal rights or responsibility of the absent State formed part of “the very subject matter” of the dispute. In its Written Statement and oral arguments (here and here), Nicaragua makes three primary arguments in response. First, the Court should narrowly interpret Monetary Gold and East Timor to render a claim inadmissible only where a party to a case claims a legal right that is also claimed by an absent State. Second, the Court can find that Germany breached various obligations of conduct without finding that this conduct resulted in Israel’s commission of illegal acts. Finally, the Court can treat as “givens” the findings contained in its provisional measures orders in South Africa v. Israel as well as in its advisory opinions of 2024 and 2025. I will not discuss Nicaragua’s primary arguments here. Instead, I will focus on an alternative argument contained in Nicaragua’s Written Statement (paras. 216-221). According to this alternative argument, the Court can find Germany responsible for failing to prevent genocide committed by certain individuals without attributing the acts of those individuals to Israel. Presumably, the individuals Nicaragua has in mind are Israeli officials, including members of Israel’s government and armed forces. Obviously, the acts of Israeli officials are attributable to Israel. But Nicaragua’s point is that the Court does not need to attribute the acts of these individuals to Israel in order to find that Germany failed to prevent these acts. The Court does not need to find Israel responsible for these acts as a prerequisite of finding Germany responsible for failing to prevent these acts. It follows that the “Monetary Gold principle” invoked by Germany does not render inadmissible Nicaragua’s claim that Germany failed to prevent genocide. Nicaragua’s alternative argument is correct. Indeed, its logic extends to Nicaragua’s claims that Germany is complicit in acts of genocide and that Germany failed to ensure respect for international humanitarian law. I discussed the latter claims more systematically in an earlier essay on Just Security. In this post, I will simply explain how Nicaragua’s alternative argument should be understood. According to Nicaragua’s alternative argument, the Court can find that Germany failed to prevent the commission of acts of genocide by certain individuals without deciding that the State of Israel is responsible for those acts. As Nicaragua explains, the responsibility of another State for genocide or genocidal acts is not a condition for finding that a State is responsible for not preventing these acts. In the Bosnian Genocide case, the Court did not determine that any State Party was responsible for having actually committed genocide. It determined that genocide was committed by individuals and groups, and that an obligation to prevent genocide arose when there was a “serious risk” of the crime being committed. This is correct. Under the Genocide Convention, genocide is an act committed by individuals, which States Parties undertake to prevent, by using whatever influence they may have over those individuals, when they become aware of a serious risk that those individuals will commit genocide. It does not matter whether the acts are performed within a State Party’s territory, or by its citizens, or in the territory of another State, or by citizens of another State, or by a non-state armed group, or by a political organization, or by the officials of another State. The obligation to prevent genocide works exactly the same way: as an obligation to prevent individuals from committing genocide. If necessary and in the alternative, if it deems it more appropriate, the Court could proceed in the same manner here: after having noted that acts of genocide have been committed, it could determine to which extent Germany has provided aid and assistance in the commission of this genocide without having to decide that the State of Israel itself is responsible for genocide. This is correct. The Court could proceed by finding that acts of genocide have been committed by individuals in Gaza, and that Germany provided aid and assistance to these individuals in their commission of genocide, or that Germany failed to use its influence over these individuals to prevent their commission of genocide. Notably, aiding or assisting individuals in their commission of genocide establishes complicity in genocide under the Genocide Convention, in contrast to aiding or assisting another State in its commission of an internationally wrongful act. As Nicaragua explains, the Court could proceed in this manner without having to decide that the State of Israel itself is responsible for genocide. In its oral argument, Germany responded that Nicaragua’s alternative argument still requires the Court to make findings of genocide, as in the Bosnian Genocide case, and there, of course, there was no third State involved, so the current issue did not arise: the genocide alleged was conducted by an entity ⎯ the Bosnian-Serb army ⎯ whose acts could not be attributed to Serbia or any other State. Here, by contrast, Nicaragua alleges breach by Germany with respect, specifically, to “the commission of genocide by Israel” …. And it is by supplying military equipment to Israel (and not to any other actor) that Nicaragua alleges that Germany is breaching its obligation of prevention. Likewise, the evidence that Nicaragua deploys purports to show the commission of a genocide by Israel, not by any other party. Germany’s response fails in at least two ways. First, it is irrelevant that Nicaragua refers to the commission of genocide by Israel in its primary arguments, since its alternative argument clearly shifts the focus to the commission of genocide by individuals. The alternative argument must be evaluated on its own terms. Second, it is beside the point that the acts of the Bosnian-Serb army were not attributed to Serbia or any other State. The point is that the responsibility of a third State (hypothetically, Russia) for failing to prevent the Bosnian-Serb army from committing genocide would depend on that third State’s influence over the Bosnian-Serb army, not on the attribution of the Bosnian-Serb army’s acts to Serbia. This is a simple point of legal logic, but it helps to illustrate with a hypothetical example. Suppose that State A has influence (short of effective control) over an armed group, and is aware of a serious risk that the armed group is about to commit genocide, but fails to use its influence to prevent the latter’s commission of genocide. Clearly, State A would be responsible for its failure to prevent genocide by the armed group. Crucially, this conclusion follows irrespective of whether the acts of the armed group are attributable to any other State. Put the other way around, the attribution or non-attribution of the acts of the armed group to another State is not a prerequisite to establishing the responsibility of State A for failure to prevent genocide by the armed group. Now suppose that the armed group in question turns out to be a covert unit of the armed forces of State B. Nothing changes. State A is still responsible for failing to prevent the commission of genocide by the unit, and this conclusion does not depend on attributing the acts of the unit to State B. Obviously, the acts of the unit are attributable to State B, since the unit turns out to be an organ of State B. But the attribution of the unit’s commission of genocide to State B is not a prerequisite to finding State A responsible for failing to prevent genocide. State A’s responsibility depends on its own failure to use its influence over the individual members of the unit. The point can also be expressed in (semi-)formal terms: P1: If a State fails to use its influence over individuals despite its awareness of a serious risk that the individuals will commit genocide, and the individuals commit genocide, then that State breaches its obligation to prevent genocide. P2: State A had influence over the unit and was aware of a serious risk that the unit would commit genocide. P3: State A failed to use its influence over the unit to prevent the unit from committing genocide. C1: Therefore, State A breached its obligation to prevent genocide. Clearly, the preceding line of reasoning does not depend on the attribution of the acts of the unit to State B, which would proceed along intersecting but distinct lines: P6: State B is responsible for acts attributed to it. The two arguments share a common premise (P4) but neither conclusion depends on the other. C1 does not depend on C2, and C2 is not a prerequisite for C1. In other words, a finding of State A’s responsibility does not depend on a finding of State B’s responsibility, and a finding of State B’s responsibility is not a prerequisite for a finding of State A’s responsibility. It follows that the Monetary Gold principle is not engaged. Nicaragua’s alternative argument is correct. The Court can find that Germany breached its obligation to prevent acts of genocide committed by individuals over whom it had influence, namely Israeli officials, without finding Israel responsible for those acts. Israel’s responsibility is not a prerequisite for Germany’s responsibility, so Israel’s responsibility is not part of the “very subject-matter” of the dispute. It follows that the Monetary Gold principle is not engaged. The logic of Nicaragua’s alternative argument extends to its claims regarding complicity in genocide and failure to ensure respect for international humanitarian law (see here). However, its logic may not extend to Nicaragua’s claims regarding denial of self-determination, racial discrimination, segregation and apartheid. While genocide may be committed by individuals and only then attributed (or not attributed) to States, these other claims involve violations of legal obligations binding on States as such. The admissibility of these other claims therefore depends on Nicaragua’s primary arguments summarized above. Nicaragua’s alternative argument is correct, but that does not mean that it will succeed. The alternative argument does not appear in Nicaragua’s Memorial, and was not mentioned in Nicaragua’s oral arguments. In Nicaragua’s 132-page Written Statement, it takes up six paragraphs. While its logic is sound, its meaning is not always clear. The Court may miss it entirely or simply not understand it. That would be a great pity, since Nicaragua’s alternative argument is correct. ©  Opinio Juris | Design by Open & Honest | In association with the International Commission of Jurists

title: Hyundai launches China-tailored Ioniq V electric sedan from under $15,000 - CnEVPost
content: Beijing Hyundai, Hyundai Motor's Chinese joint venture, has launched the Ioniq V with competitive entry pricing and more trim options to compete in China's electric sedan market. The mid-size sedan went on sale on Tuesday, with 5 variants at limited-time prices ranging from 99,900 yuan ($14,820) to 131,900 yuan. Suggested retail prices range from 109,900 yuan to 139,900 yuan, with limited-time launch discounts of 8,000 yuan or 10,000 yuan, depending on the variant. The model opened for pre-sales at the Chengdu Auto Show in August with 3 variants priced between 119,900 yuan and 139,900 yuan. The launch adds the entry-level 540 Pro and long-range 650 Max. The new entry-level variant and limited-time discounts bring the Ioniq V's starting price 20,000 yuan below its pre-sales starting price. The Ioniq V is the first production model since Hyundai introduced the Ioniq brand in China this year. Its performance will test the South Korean automaker's renewed electrification strategy in the country. Led by Hyundai's China design center, the sedan was developed for Chinese customers and is also intended for other markets. It is the production version of the Venus Concept unveiled at the Beijing Auto Show in April. The Ioniq V features a fastback design and frameless doors. It measures 4,900 mm in length, 1,890 mm in width and 1,470 mm in height, with a wheelbase of 2,900 mm. Built on E-GMP (Electric Global Modular Platform), the model offers single-motor versions with peak outputs of 140 kW (188 hp) and 168 kW, and supports 800-volt fast charging. CATL (HKEX: 3750) supplies the lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries, available in capacities of 53.48 kWh and 66.85 kWh. CLTC range options are 540 km and 650 km. The sedan's technology features reflect Hyundai's growing use of China's supply chain. The cabin has a 27-inch 4K screen and a Qualcomm Snapdragon 8295P chip, with a head-up display also available. The infotainment system integrates AI models including Baidu's Ernie Bot and ByteDance's Doubao. It supports independent voice control across 4 zones in the front and rear, continuous dialogue and multiple commands. For driver assistance, the Ioniq V offers an L2+ system developed with Momenta (HKEX: 6880), featuring highway navigation assistance, urban memory navigation assistance and parking assistance. Beijing Hyundai is also offering a lifetime vehicle warranty as part of its launch benefits, along with battery replacement for degradation and compensation for spontaneous battery fires, subject to time and mileage limits, to bolster buyer confidence. When Hyundai formally introduced the Ioniq brand in China in April, it outlined plans to launch 20 battery electric vehicle (BEV) and extended-range electric vehicle (EREV) models locally over the next 5 years. The company aims to expand its China business to 500,000 vehicles by 2030 through local development and partnerships with Chinese suppliers. title: Brazil line-up and where to watch the friendly v Australia - Yahoo Sports
content: Four days after the 1-1 draw in the city of Townsville, the Brazil national team returns to action this Tuesday (29) to face Australia in Brisbane. Head coach Carlo Ancelotti has prepared changes to the starting lineup and tactical setup in search of a win in the second test of this first FIFA window of the new World Cup cycle. After avoiding defeat only in stoppage time in the first match (with a goal from youngster Rayan), Ancelotti will make seven changes to the starting team and adopt a 4-3-3 formation. The coach's big gamble is moving Raphinha into the center-forward role, replicating the position in which the player has stood out at Barcelona at the start of this season. The defensive system has been completely revamped with the additions of Otávio, Vanderson, Jair, Gabriel Magalhães and Mauro Júnior. In midfield, Gabriel Bontempo joins Danilo and Bruno Guimarães. During the press conference, Ancelotti played down the pressure. "The criticism affects what I think about the future zero. I really liked the young players who are here. We have a future, despite the criticism." Australia's current moment On the Australian side, head coach Tony Popovic praised his team's performance in the first meeting and wants to prove that the "Socceroos" can maintain a competitive level against elite national teams. According to Popovic, the biggest challenge will be making up for the squad's lesser international experience and delivering a second straight strong performance against a Brazil side that will try to erase the poor impression left on Friday. This will be the 10th meeting in history between Brazil and Australia. The advantage is heavily in favor of the Brazil national team, which has six wins, two draws and only one defeat against their Oceanian rivals. title: BTS Member V Joins Nothing as Global Brand Ambassador - dscene magazine
content: Nothing has named V, also known as Kim Taehyung of BTS, as its new Global Brand Ambassador. The partnership begins with a campaign shot in Seoul by photographer Dorothea Sing Zhang and introduces the brand’s Headphone (1) Pro, its latest premium over-ear model. The campaign places V within a visual concept focused on experimentation, movement and creative expression. Nothing developed the project around the relationship between artistic instinct and technical design, positioning V as a natural partner for its approach to audio. The shoot includes Ear (3a), Headphone (1), Headphone (a) and Ear (3), extending the partnership beyond a single product launch. For the campaign concept, Nothing looked toward music videos and moving-image experiments that place movement at the center of performance. The brand referenced Jamiroquai’s “Virtual Insanity,” Gene Kelly’s “Singin’ in the Rain” and the work of Spike Lee. Eadweard Muybridge’s early experiments with sequential photography also informed the visual direction, with layered images of V used to suggest movement and creative process. Music became another part of the development. Nothing wanted a track that reflected V’s versatility, with jazz entering the conversation before the team considered George Michael and Spandau Ballet. They eventually selected Suzanne Vega’s “Tom’s Diner.” Headphone (1) Pro arrives as Nothing’s most advanced audio product to date. The over-ear headphones use a triple-driver architecture designed to separate bass, midrange and treble reproduction. The system includes a 40mm bass driver alongside dedicated midrange and xMEMS treble drivers, with a frequency response extending from 20Hz to 40kHz. Nothing also equips the model with its strongest active noise cancellation system so far, using ten microphones. The headphones support high-resolution audio and LDAC, while a Flat EQ mode developed with London’s Metropolis Studios gives users an option designed around more neutral listening. Dynamic Spatial Audio adds another listening mode to the package. The exterior continues Nothing’s transparent industrial approach through visible elements, glass panels and metal details. The headphones support wired listening through a 3.5mm connection and USB-C alongside wireless playback. Battery life reaches up to 68 hours with active noise cancellation switched off. V’s appointment expands Nothing’s growing relationship with musicians. Earlier in 2026, Charli xcx joined the company as its first Global Brand Ambassador and shareholder. The addition of V gives the brand another major music figure as it develops its presence across audio, design and contemporary culture. content: Subscribe for full access to The Hollywood Reporter Subscribe for full access to The Hollywood Reporter Praised Nothing co-founder and CEO Carl Pei: "V has an instinct for fearless experimentation. He's always pushing into different sounds and styles." The BTS superstar has joined the tech-forward accessories company as its latest global ambassador, and he debuts by starring in a new campaign modeling Nothing’s new Headphone (1) Pro. Shot in Seoul by Dorothea Sing Zhang, the campaign was fashioned to spotlight the “experimentation and versatility of authentic expression” while reflecting a celebration of technical excellence for both partners. Described by Nothing as the brand’s “most advanced audio product to date,” the Headphone (1) Pro features a triple-driver architecture comprising a 40-mm bass dynamic driver, a precision dynamic driver and a treble xMEMS driver to deliver detail and immersion across a frequency response range of 20Hz-40kHz. title: This Is Not a Feature Vector: Zentian v. Apple - Patently-O
content:
The Federal Circuit has affirmed the PTAB's cancellation of all six claims of Zentian's speech-recognition patent in a short nonprecedential opinion. Zentian Ltd. v. Apple Inc., No. 2024-2205 (Fed. Cir. Sept. 25, 2026). Vector quantization: Jiang computes a feature vector for each short frame of audio, then swaps it for the closest entry in a codebook built in advance from training data. The codeword is itself a multi-component vector, a stand-in for a whole cluster of similar feature vectors. The swap gives up a little precision to save a lot of computation. U.S. Patent No. 10,062,377 covers a speech-recognition system that splits the work across separate devices. The first device slices incoming audio into short time frames and converts each frame into a "feature vector," a set of numbers that places that sound as a point in N-dimensional space. A second device calculates the "distance" between each feature vector and the states of an acoustic model, and a third uses those distances (with Hidden Markov Models or neural networks and a lexical tree of words) to identify what was said.  The whole appeal turned on one term: "feature vector." Claim 1 requires requires word identification using distances "calculated from a first feature vector." Apple's lead reference (Jiang) calculates those distances from vector-quantized "codewords" instead. The patentee Zentian argued that a codeword is not a feature vector. The Board and the court disagreed, relying mostly on the claim's own definition of a feature vector as comprising "extracted and/or derived quantities from said digital audio stream." The case itself is largely a mill run, but it includes an interesting invocation of René Magritte's 1929 painting The Treachery of Images, the beautifully rendered tobacco pipe over the caption "Ceci n'est pas une pipe." In Zentian's words: "Just as a painting of a pipe is not a pipe, 'representations' of feature vectors are not feature vectors." Apple answered with a pipe analogy of its own -- that the prior art codeword was like "choosing one pipe to represent a group of similar pipes." Their point -- that the court accepted -- was that a codeword isn't a painting of a feature vector. Rather, It's a real feature vector picked from the codebook to stand in for a cluster of similar ones. To continue reading, become a Patently-O member. Already a member? title: NATHAN v. TRUMP – Birthright Citizenship Part II - ACLU of DC
content: Soon after the Supreme Court ruled that President Trump’s Executive Order seeking to do away with birthright citizenship was unconstitutional, he tried again, with a new Executive Order, issued on August 6, 2026, that directs executive agencies not to recognize the citizenship of an individual “when neither parent of that person is a citizen” and: a) “either parent of that person is an alien enemy, defined to include” a member of certain designated terrorist organizations; b) “either parent of that person is a foreign government employee,” including not only foreign ministers with full diplomatic immunity but also various other employees of foreign governments or international organizations; c) “either parent of that person engaged in a commercial transaction to purchase or access birthright citizenship for the person, or engaged in fraudulent activity to obtain citizenship”; or d) “the person is born in a territory or territorial waters of the United States where citizenship is not conferred by Federal statute.” On September 28, 2026, we and the National ACLU filed a new lawsuit challenging the new Executive Order. We allege that it is unconstitutional for the same reasons the first one was, and that it also violates the federal immigration statute, as Justice Kavanaugh opined was true of the first order. We will soon file a motion for a preliminary injunction asking the court to prevent executive agencies from refusing to recognize the citizenship of our clients’ children and others similarly situated.
